title: Breaking And Entering: Weyes Blood
summary: Natalie Mering aka Weyes Blood is bringing her doomsday dream-pop to Australia this June. Ahead of her tour and two headlining shows at RISING, Natalie joins Lauren for a wide-ranging conversation on Breaking And Entering.
transcript:
Lauren Taylor spoke with Natalie Mering, who records as Weyes Blood, ahead of her June 2023 Australian tour and two shows at Melbourne's RISING festival. Presented on Breaking and Entering on 25 May 2023, the conversation explores her fifth album, And in the Darkness, Hearts Aglow, the second in a trilogy that began with 2019's Titanic Rising. Mering had previously visited Triple R in February 2020, when she was in Australia for Golden Plains.

[Music]

Lauren: Weyes Blood's music has such a timeless quality, and echoes of '60s folk and '70s West Coast AM radio, and themes that grapple with modern issues like the climate crisis and the difficulty in finding genuine connection among a generation that are living their lives almost entirely online. Natalie has described 'It's Not Just Me, It's Everybody' as a Buddhist anthem, ensconced in the interconnectivity of all things and the fraying of our social fabric. It seems to be a really central preoccupation of this new album, that Buddhist idea of the interconnectivity of all things. So I began my chat with Weyes Blood by asking Natalie why that's something she feels so compelled to explore.

Natalie: Yeah, I think that I'm kind of constantly trying to reconcile all the different esoteric interpretations of reality because I was raised Christian, and Buddhism is kind of like the forbidden fruit for me. Finding the relationship between the cosmology I grew up with and Buddhism, and how that applies to modern thought as well, I just think it's very important and elemental. And if you're going to think about human consciousness, inevitably these are the concepts that are going to come up, because it's still up for debate if we're all actually separate, in my opinion.

Lauren: Finding the light in the darkness can come from human connection as well, can't it? It's always felt like an important theme in your work and something you've been exploring for a really long time. Conversely, we've spoken about connection, but also feeling isolation and chaos as well, and exploring themes of disconnection with your work with Weyes Blood too. The film clip for the track we just spoke about earlier, 'It's Not Just Me, It's Everybody', does touch on technology and its role in both connecting and disconnecting us. The video, for those who maybe haven't seen, features yourself dancing with this animated cartoon phone that essentially goes around murdering people. But I think you summed it up as—

Natalie: Eating people.

Lauren: Yes. You summed it up as technological cannibalism, and that it's harvesting our attention away from each other. Can you tell us about your ways of finding focus and how you maintain maybe healthy tech boundaries in your life? How do you switch off? How do you recharge? I mean, you're touring a lot. How do you recharge when you're on tour?

Natalie: Well, luckily, it doesn't come super naturally to me. I'm right on that weird generational brink where it's like I'm not the biggest social media person. And I don't find a lot of solace, per se, in internet culture, which I have friends that are my age that do. So it's kind of a random assignment, I guess, but I just got the Gen X assignment. It doesn't totally resonate with me. But I do feel like it still occupies a lot of my time, and it's kind of how I get news and different things like that. So I kind of just get sick of it. And I don't know, I unfortunately don't have the same kind of relationship with it that I think a young person does.

[Music]

Lauren: Natalie, I understand that one book you were reading that you reference in that letter accompanying the new record is by cultural historian Christopher Lasch, from 1979, the book The Culture of Narcissism. And I understand that book served as one of the key inspirations for your recent inquiries into the fragmented nature of our social lives. Maybe for those who aren't familiar, can you tell us a bit about the book, and what were some of the main takeaways? Why did it inspire this new record?

Natalie: Yeah. The Culture of Narcissism for me was just a cool eye-opener in terms of the myth of Narcissus, which was something that I think we notoriously misinterpret, where we kind of think that he was so vain that he was obsessed with his own reflection in the mirror, when in reality he didn't recognise that it was himself. And I think that that's something the human race really contends with a lot, where it's like we are kind of desperately grasping and searching for something outside of ourselves that will only be accomplished from going within. And so I think that that's kind of what 'God Turn Me Into a Flower' is about, and what people commonly miss about narcissism. I feel like most people talk about the vanity aspect of it and not the confusion.

Lauren: Have you thought much about, I know it's an enormous subject, but overcoming narcissism in our modern age? Was that something you were thinking about?

Natalie: Well, I think the first thing that needs to be overcome in the modern age is the systems of exchanging information are so disrupted that people don't really know how to talk to each other exactly anymore. There's not a lot of great public discourse spaces for nuanced conversation. I just sense that there's a difficulty in communicating, which I think would certainly be a healing salve for people to feel more connected to one another, and responsible to one another, and kind of less in their own hall of mirrors. But I do think that the modern life and the modern civilisation caters towards a certain degree of isolation, and I think that that is maybe the beginning of the narcissism. Not so much like we're just all naturally inherently narcissistic, taking a bunch of selfies. I think the selfie is a cry out for help, you know. So I think there's things that preclude the narcissistic tendencies, and reasons why we became narcissistic that have their roots back many generations.

[Music]

Lauren: Natalie, those themes of social decay we've been speaking about can ultimately be addressed by going beyond that selfish ambition and placing more of our focus on community and coming together. I was wondering if you could speak about the importance of community in your life and in the work that you do.

Natalie: I mean, I love when I have a community. It means so much to me. It's like a homecoming, because I tend to be more on the rugged individualist side of things, I think as an American and as somebody that's a musician that used to travel solo and do a lot of things alone. I do kind of have a lone wolf mentality, and when I do find a community of musicians, it's usually kind of a phase. It'll be a certain city I lived in six years ago, and there was the six months where everybody was just on fire and making a lot of music together, hanging out, or going on a long tour with my crew and my band and really bonding, or making a record. So the community is kind of constantly evolving and shifting around because I bounce around a lot. So I kind of maintain a lone wolf status, but like to engage with communities.

Natalie: And I will say that over the course of my 11 years or whatever playing music professionally, the community used to be a little bit more defined, because I think there was just more that people kind of did of their own volition. And there was this certain turning point where it became more about being internet based, or kind of trying to go for a piece of the pie, as opposed to setting up DIY shows or house shows, and playing with your friends, and doing these little crummy tours for nobody, and slowly meeting people and building up this momentum from just experience. And I think a lot of people nowadays are kind of in the dawn of the death of a lot of DIY venues. It's almost like you kind of have to, out of the gates, have a more professional quality. And I would say that it's almost like DIY music has been stripped of some of its naivety from the internet and stuff. The idea that you could be at a show and it's the centre of the world because you don't have a phone to show you otherwise. So the phones, I think, decentralised communities where people used to kind of congregate and meet up and not really think [Unclear audio at 00:17:52–00:17:59]. And I think the phones really generate that kind of attitude where you'll be at a show and people will be on their phone or thinking about somewhere else they could be, and just genuinely a little less engaged. And I mean, I don't know, maybe I'm going to the wrong shows, but this is just something that I've noticed. And this is not necessarily for big concerts. When you get to a big concert, everybody really wants to be there. I'm talking about developmental touring and being a kind of a nobody band who's just starting out for the first time. And those kinds of communities used to be so nourishing and helpful, and I think they're more disparate maybe than they were in the past.

[Music]

Lauren: Last time you were in Australia, we spoke to you on the show. You actually came into the Triple R studios, and you were visiting Australia at the very end of February 2020 and talking about Titanic Rising, and some of the themes around your previous record being feelings of impending doom. And you spoke to us of being already mentally preparing yourself for an apocalypse or a terrible thing at the time of writing that record. Do you feel like you were tapping into something that was collectively maybe about to come at the time of writing your last record, maybe a weird premonition or something at the time perhaps?

Natalie: Definitely. I think I have a pretty decent gut instinct that I've been learning about over time, and I could just kind of sense that was the vibe. I think that's maybe how a lot of people felt but didn't know yet. And the pandemic was a bit like truth serum, like gasoline pouring on the fire or something. But yeah, I think that I've always been a very sensitive person in that way.

Lauren: There was certainly still a hopeful element to that album, to Titanic Rising, and even an optimistic kind of quality to the word rising, even in the title. You've said previously that you think it's very important for people to still have hope and to not be scared, and that through your work you're definitely trying to shed light on matters and comfort people and make sure everyone has each other's backs. I'm interested in how this new record relates to that, and the title, for example, And in the Darkness, Hearts Aglow. There's a letter accompanying the release of the new record, and you liken your heart to a glow stick that's been cracked. And there's obviously that really powerful image that you've used on the cover of your record too. Would you describe this new album as a hopeful record yet? Or given it's the second album in a trilogy, where are we at with this phase?

Natalie: I feel like it's kind of like the music that was made amidst the blare of the alarm. It's like the kind of purgatory where it was like, now there's no question that these things are in place and happening. So what does that do to our social fabric and to our concepts of intimacy, and kind of living amongst it, in the thick of it? And I find it to be a little bit more of an introverted record, and more introspective and kind of subterranean in terms of the journey inward.

[Music]
